unlisted_practices: Choose privacy-enhancing technologies that avoid vulnerabilities by design, such as statistics-based federated learning, over approaches that require added safeguards, where possible.
Define governance frameworks that explicitly specify who controls data, who authorizes analysis, who benefits from resulting models, and how communities are represented in decision-making.
Develop AI tools with local communities, not merely from their data.

International bodies, funders, journals, and regulators should develop harmonized guidance that distinguishes privacy-preserving model training from traditional data transfer and establishes proportionate safeguards based on what information is actually shared.
Adopt common data models and consistent terminology to standardize data structures across sites and facilitate cross-institutional collaboration.
Invest in foundational digital health data systems before adopting privacy-enhancing technologies in settings where health data remain undigitized.

Invest in lightweight AI models that run on standard clinical hardware or mobile devices, open-source tooling with clear documentation, and capacity-building initiatives that transfer expertise as well as models.
Build AI partnerships on mutual benefit, including local capacity building, shared authorship, technology transfer, and tangible improvements in local healthcare delivery.
Co-create AI tools with local providers, patients, and communities so they reflect local needs and values.
Do not use privacy-enhancing technologies as a superficial ethical badge or compliance shortcut that bypasses meaningful consent, community governance, or ongoing accountability.
Design and adopt privacy-enhancing technologies as digital public goods.
Adapt large language models locally to low-resource contexts using parameter-efficient fine-tuning, such as LoRA, and quantization to reduce computational requirements.
Deploy open-weights LLMs locally with attention to safety guardrails and compliance with institutional policies on model provenance.
Apply differential privacy during LLM fine-tuning to limit memorization of individual patient records.
Govern access to retrieval databases carefully in retrieval-augmented generation and protect retrieved content if external LLMs are used.
Validate synthetic data to ensure that statistical properties and clinical utility are preserved.
Address transparency, accountability, fairness, and safety alongside privacy in responsible AI.

screen.reason: This is a perspective piece outlining priorities and recommendations for implementing privacy-enhancing technologies for equitable global health AI.
